title: Hope
tomorrow: what does love actually do on an ordinary Tuesday?

cards: A scratch-off ticket on the fridge. Fingers crossed before a test. A text you keep refreshing.
That's wishful thinking: it leans on one outcome, and if the outcome doesn't come, it falls over. Paul says Christian hope is built differently.

In his letter to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "And hope confoundeth not: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts." Confoundeth not: it doesn't put you to shame, doesn't leave you stranded.
Wishful thinking can. So what's the difference? It's something you can feel in your hands.

teach.b: Hold something heavy for a moment: a book, a full mug, a stone. Feel it pull down.
The Letter to the Hebrews picks exactly that kind of object for hope, in the Douay-Rheims: "Which we have as an anchor of the soul, sure and firm." Look at what an anchor does and doesn't do.
It doesn't stop the storm. It doesn't promise calm water. It keeps the boat from drifting while the waves do whatever they do.

teach.h: TIED TO A PERSON, NOT A RESULT.
teach.b: Wishful thinking is tied to a result: the test, the score, the call back. Christian hope is tied to a person.
The Catechism describes it as trusting Christ's promises and leaning not on your own strength but on the help of the Holy Spirit.
Paul's reason is in that same verse from Romans: hope holds because God's love has already been poured in. It's not a forecast. It's a weight that's already on the sea floor.

teach.h: AN ANCHOR CARVED ON A GRAVE.
teach.b: One to tell a friend tonight: in the catacombs of Rome, some Christian graves carry a carved anchor, and some readers see a cross hidden in its shape. People burying those they loved chose that sign.
Hope, here, doesn't mean everything will turn out the way you want. It means you won't be cut loose when it doesn't.

how: Catholics name hope as one of the three theological virtues, with faith and charity; some pray a short traditional Act of Hope, and the anchor appears as a Christian sign of hope in art and on graves.

o: trust in God's promises that holds through anything
a wish for luck said before something hard
confidence that things will work out your way

s: Christian hope means trusting that things will turn out the way you want
an anchor doesn't stop the storm. hope means you aren't cut loose when things go wrong.
Hebrews calls hope an anchor of the soul
"an anchor of the soul, sure and firm."
for Paul, hope holds because of how strong your own feelings are
Romans 5:5 says it holds because God's love has been poured into the heart.

games.q: your cousin's surgery is next week. she says, "i'm hoping it goes fine." on the Catholic view of hope, what's under that sentence?
o: a forecast that the odds are good.
a hold on God that stays, however it goes.
a wish that stops if the news is bad.
games.why: Hebrews calls hope an anchor: it doesn't stop the storm, it keeps you from drifting. the Catechism ties it to trusting Christ's promises, not the odds.

practice: Keep the heavy thing resting in your palm, and press your feet into the floor. Name one thing you're unsure about, and let it rock like a wave while your hand and feet stay put.
If you pray, you can say the two words of an act of hope, I hope, and let the weight in your hand say the rest.

wordCard.voice: Hope. An anchor of the soul: not a promise of calm water, but a hold that keeps you from drifting.

orig.note: Greek: hope. the word in Romans 5:5 and Hebrews 6:19.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: I hope, an anchor that holds even while the boat is still rocking. See you tomorrow.
